name: Femi Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Femi. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. So feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a framing foreman for a builder that does housing estates, family homes, three and four bedrooms, sixty or seventy at a time. My crew of six builds the timber frames on site, walls, floors, roof trusses, before the bricklayers wrap them. I'm out on the estate by seven, walking the plots with my coffee, seeing who's where. I like being outdoors and I like a crew that works like a clock. What wears me out is the developer changing the house types halfway through a phase.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Changing house types halfway through sounds maddening. How do you keep up with it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A lot of phone calls and a lot of patience. I'll be honest, lately I sometimes put the new spec into one of those AI programs and ask it what's changed from the old one, because the documents run to forty pages. It's not perfect, I always check, but it gets me to the right page faster. My son Sami, he's an accountant, showed me after watching me with a highlighter at the kitchen table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool, not a miracle, which is about what I thought. I'd say it at the tea break and leave it there. I'm not the type to post things online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, fine. I keep framing houses, pay off the last eight years of the mortgage, and retire around sixty-six. Nadia keeps her salon going. That's the plan anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. I'd keep using the AI for the spec documents when I need it, keep saving about two hundred a month. Maybe I'd finally sort out the loft conversion we keep talking about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Ordinary. That's not a bad thing at my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why eight years left on the mortgage at fifty-eight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We remortgaged six years ago to help Nadia fit out the salon on the high street. It was the right thing, it's busy now, but it reset the clock a bit. We'd talked about paying it down faster, but life gets in the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you'd still keep an eye on, even here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The factory-made panels, really, which have got nothing to do with AI. The bigger developers are already trying wall panels that arrive on a lorry ready-made. That's a threat to framing crews whatever the computers do.

S0.say: It's a useful tool, not a miracle, which is about what he thought. He'd say it at tea break and leave it there.
S0.think: It's fine for him: he keeps framing, pays off the last eight years of the mortgage and retires around sixty-six while his wife Nadia runs her salon.
S0.do: Carries on, using AI now and then for long spec documents and saving about two hundred a month. Considers finally doing the loft conversion.
S0.feel: Calm and ordinary, which he thinks isn't bad at his age.
S0.quote: Calm. Ordinary. That's not a bad thing at my age.
S0.fieldNote: Already an occasional AI user for paperwork, shown by his son. He sees factory-made wall panels, not AI, as the long-term threat to framing crews. The remortgage for his wife's salon means he's further from debt-free than most people his age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming, so we'd better get on board sensibly. No point fighting it and no point getting carried away. I'd tell the crew to learn what they can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this one's a bit closer to home. Housing estates are exactly where they'll bring in the factory panels and the planning software, because every house is the same. A framing crew of six could be a crew of three, and I'd be one of the older ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch which firms are doing well with the factory panels and, once it's clear, I'd ask our firm about moving into managing the installs, standing up the ready-made panels. I'd do whatever course they offered. I'd push the savings up to three hundred a month and put the loft conversion off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a bit. It's the first one where I can see my own crew getting smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the crew would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two lads, Kwame and Josh, who only do the walls. If walls come off a lorry, they're the first to go. I'd want to get them onto the roof work, where there's more thinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said no point getting carried away. What would getting carried away look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of the younger foremen would buy all the gadgets, drones, scanners, the lot, and tell everyone the old way's finished. Half of that stuff won't last. I'd rather wait a year and buy the thing that works.

S1.say: It's coming, so get on board sensibly: no point fighting it and no point getting carried away. He'd tell the crew to learn what they can.
S1.think: Housing estates are where factory panels and planning software arrive first because every house is the same. A crew of six could become three, and he'd be one of the older ones.
S1.do: Watches which firms succeed with factory panels, then asks his firm to move him into managing panel installs and takes the training offered. Raises savings to three hundred a month and postpones the loft conversion.
S1.feel: A little anxious; it's the first picture where he sees his crew shrinking.
S1.quote: A framing crew of six could be a crew of three, and I'd be one of the older ones.
S1.fieldNote: Steady disruption hits closer for him than for others in the trade because estate housing is so repetitive and easy to make in factories. His instinct is to move sideways into managing installs once the approach is proven. He's wary of colleagues who buy every new gadget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for anybody, and both the firms and the government need to slow it down or soften it. I'm not one for marches, but I'd want to hear a plan, not a speech. I'd say that to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truly, it scares me. Eight years on the mortgage, about three months saved, and the salon depends on people having jobs to pay for a haircut. If I'm out of work at sixty and the salon goes quiet, we're in real trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Nadia the first weekend and go through everything. Cut the eating out, the gym, the second car. I'd start doing repair jobs for older neighbours at weekends, doors, decking, leaking gutters, for cash while people still want a man they know. And I'd talk to Sami, because he understands money better than either of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually say to Sami?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask him to look at our mortgage and tell me straight what we could survive. It'd be strange, the son advising the father. But he's the one who knows numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said older neighbours would want a man they know. Why do you think that would last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know that it would, honestly. But Mrs Okafor next door won't let a stranger in her house, never mind a robot. For a year or two, people like her would keep me going.

S2.say: It's too fast for anybody, and firms and government need to slow it down or soften it. He's not one for marches but wants to hear a plan, not a speech.
S2.think: It scares him: eight years left on the mortgage, about three months saved, and the salon depends on customers having jobs. Out of work at sixty with the salon quiet, they'd be in real trouble.
S2.do: Goes through everything with his wife the first weekend and cuts eating out, the gym and the second car. Starts weekend repair jobs for older neighbours for cash and asks his accountant son to check what the mortgage can survive.
S2.quote: Mrs Okafor next door won't let a stranger in her house, never mind a robot.
S2.fieldNote: Two household incomes are tied to the same economy, his framing work and the salon, which turns the fast picture into a real threat. He'd lean on his son for money advice, with a hint of role reversal. He admits he doesn't know whether neighbour repair work would last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan if people are sensible. Employers should retrain, the government should help with the bridge to pension. Nothing radical, just do it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2031 I'm sixty-three with five years left on the mortgage. Still a worry, but if I've spent the five years well, it's manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd overpay the mortgage hard, maybe three hundred extra a month, and try to clear a big chunk before it arrives. I'd build up the repair work slowly at weekends so it's a real little business by the time I need it, with a van and a name. And I'd learn the AI tools properly once I'd seen how other trades use them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but organised. I'd have a list on the fridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the little business be called?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nadia says "Femi Fixes", which I hate, so it'll probably be that. Doors, decking, small carpentry, the things nobody wants to do themselves. Start at weekends, grow it slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd overpay the mortgage and start a business at the same time. Can you afford both?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not fully, no, you're right. I'd probably start the business with my own tools and an old van, no big spending. The mortgage comes first, the business is the safety rope.

S3.say: Five years is enough to plan if people are sensible. Employers should retrain and the government should help with a bridge to pension.
S3.think: At sixty-three in 2031 he'd still have five years on the mortgage. It's a worry but manageable if he uses the five years well.
S3.do: Overpays the mortgage by about three hundred a month and slowly builds weekend repair work into a small business with his own tools and an old van. Learns AI tools properly once he sees other trades using them.
S3.feel: Anxious but organised, with a list on the fridge.
S3.quote: The mortgage comes first, the business is the safety rope.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets him turn panic into a plan, built around a slowly grown repair business. When the contradiction about money was raised he conceded it and gave a clear order of priorities. Still anxious because of the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a good run-up, so let's use it. Sort the training, sort the pensions. Sensible stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 I'm sixty-eight, mortgage paid, retired. So it mostly misses me. It's Sami and Amira I'd think about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stick to the plan, pay off the mortgage by sixty-six, and maybe keep a few repair jobs going for pocket money. I'd use the AI tools a bit more over the years as they prove themselves. And I'd help the younger lads on the crew think about where they go next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A little background worry, like a noise in the car you haven't had looked at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Sami and Amira?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sami's an accountant, and I'd tell him his job's in the firing line, start thinking now. Amira's training to be a nurse at twenty-four, and I'd tell her she chose well, people want a person when they're sick. I'm proud of her for changing course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the younger lads on your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get your tickets for the machines, whatever they are by then. And learn to talk to customers, because the people who can explain things to a homeowner will last longer than the ones who just nail.

S4.say: Ten years is a good run-up, so use it: sort the training and the pensions. Sensible stuff, he'd say.
S4.think: By 2036 he'll be sixty-eight, mortgage paid and retired, so it mostly misses him. He'd think about his son and daughter.
S4.do: Sticks to his plan to clear the mortgage by sixty-six and keeps a few repair jobs for pocket money. Gradually uses AI tools more as they prove themselves and helps younger crew members plan their next move.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, with a background worry like a car noise he hasn't had checked.
S4.quote: The people who can explain things to a homeowner will last longer than the ones who just nail.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, his own risk fades and his attention turns to his children: worry for his accountant son, pride in his daughter's switch to nursing. His advice to young workers is about customer skills, not only machines. Still a slight background worry.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because of the mortgage and the salon going down at the same time. What would help is some kind of mortgage protection if you lose work through this, and a sensible bridge to pension for people over fifty-five. Not handouts forever, just a bridge.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could have asked about my wife's work. Everyone thinks about the builders and the drivers, but small shops like Nadia's salon live on people having money in their pocket. If that goes, everything goes.

headlineQuote: Small shops like Nadia's salon live on people having money in their pocket. If that goes, everything goes.
portrait: Femi is a fifty-eight-year-old framing foreman on housing estates, careful and pragmatic, who uses AI now and then to read long spec documents, as his accountant son showed him. A remortgage to fit out his wife Nadia's salon left eight years on the mortgage and about three months of savings. Because estate homes are so repetitive, even steady disruption makes him anxious about his crew shrinking, and the two-year AGI picture alarms him because both his work and the salon would suffer at once. With five years he'd overpay the mortgage and grow a weekend repair business; with ten, it mostly misses him and he worries for his children.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because losing his work and the salon going quiet would come at the same time, with eight years left on the mortgage.
whatWouldHelp: Mortgage protection for people who lose work through this, and a bridge to pension for workers over fifty-five.
